clue.text: Battle for job, over last fifty years or so

indicators.note: in this clue the job is placed over, ahead of, the battle in the entry

parts.note: a post is a job or position
war is battle on a grand scale

explanation.surface: Someone fighting to win a position, a struggle lasting half a century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over' sets the job before the battle. The definition is loose: the era after the Second World War, roughly half a century before this 2002 puzzle.
explanation.definitionFit: The period following the Second World War spanned roughly the fifty years before the puzzle was set.

clue.text: Dad's attempt to make a cake

parts.note: Pa is an informal name for a father, so Dad's gives PA'S
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: Father having a go at baking.
explanation.definitionFit: A Danish or similar baked sweet item is often called a pastry, a kind of small cake.

clue.text: Draw second boat

parts.note: a ketch is a two-masted sailing boat

explanation.surface: An instruction to make a picture of another vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw roughly is to make a quick outline picture.

clue.text: Poet's language has value

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', so the clue reads 'poet is'

parts.note: words, as in choice of words, means language
worth means value

explanation.surface: A remark that a poet's diction is worth something.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's on 'Poet' is 'is', linking the definition to the wordplay; William WORDSWORTH was the English Romantic poet.
explanation.definitionFit: William Wordsworth was a famous English Romantic writer of verse, author of the daffodils lines.

clue.text: Setting up bar for party

indicators.note: in a down clue, setting up means the word for bar is written upwards, from bottom to top

parts.note: a lever is a bar used to prise things

explanation.surface: Putting up a bar ready for a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setting up' reads LEVER from the bottom of a down entry, giving REVEL.
explanation.definitionFit: To revel is to make merry, as at a festive gathering; party here is a verb.

clue.text: Come shortly to way between mountains in range

indicators.note: said shortly, the word come loses its final letter

parts.note: a pass is a route through a mountain range

explanation.surface: Arrive soon at the gap between peaks in a mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shortly' cuts the last letter from COME to give COM.
explanation.definitionFit: Compass means scope or extent, as in the compass of a voice.

clue.text: Glutton crashed new motorcar

indicators.note: a crashed car is wrecked, so these letters are smashed into a new order

explanation.surface: A greedy driver wrecks a brand new car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crashed' rearranges N with MOTORCAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A cormorant is a voracious seabird, so the word is used figuratively for a greedy eater.

clue.text: Wet way to defend castle

parts.note: a watery defence: the water-filled ditch dug around a fortress

explanation.surface: A soggy method of keeping a fortress safe.
explanation.definitionFit: A water-filled trench surrounding a fortification kept attackers away from the walls.

clue.text: Harsh fall that may damage trees

definitions.text: Harsh fall that may damage trees

parts.words: Harsh fall that may damage trees
parts.note: the fall is rainfall, made harsh by pollution, which harms forests

explanation.surface: A severe drop, perhaps from a height, that could hurt woodland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fall' suggests autumn or a tumble; here it is precipitation, polluted enough to be corrosive.
explanation.definitionFit: Precipitation polluted by sulphur and nitrogen oxides is corrosive and kills forests.

clue.text: Working very hard, getting a sort of sickness

definitions.meaning: toiling so hard that one perspires
the ... sickness was a deadly epidemic disease in Tudor England

explanation.surface: Someone toiling hard and falling ill.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'sweating sickness' was a mysterious epidemic of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century England.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard toil makes one perspire, and the Tudor epidemic was named for the heavy perspiration it caused.

clue.text: About time prophet became guide

indicators.note: about means around, so the prophet's word goes around the letter for time

parts.note: a seer is a prophet

explanation.surface: Over time a prophet turned into a leader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts SEER around T.
explanation.definitionFit: To steer is to direct a course, a synonym of guide as a verb.

clue.text: Relatives turned out to be adaptable

indicators.note: turned out suggests the letters are tipped out and rearranged

explanation.surface: Family members proved flexible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned out' rearranges the letters of RELATIVES.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone versatile can turn to many tasks, which is to be flexible.

clue.text: Fish staggers in front of tree — not dead

indicators.note: the staggering word goes ahead of the tree word

parts.note: rocks means sways or staggers

indicators.note: not means the letter for dead is left out of the tree

parts.note: the almond is a tree

explanation.surface: A fish reels in front of a tree, still alive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes D (dead) from ALMOND, leaving ALMON. ROCK SALMON is a British fishmonger's name for dogfish.
explanation.definitionFit: Rock salmon is a trade name for dogfish or similar species sold in British fish shops.

clue.text: Badly-behaved child's underclothing beginning to tear

definitions.note: the 's stands for 'is', linking definition to wordplay

parts.note: a bra is an item of underwear

indicators.note: beginning to means only the first letter of the following word is used

explanation.surface: A naughty youngster's underwear starts to rip.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's on 'child' is 'is', joining definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A brat is a spoilt, unruly youngster.

clue.text: Home — see man to it, drunk

indicators.note: a drunk person staggers about, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone told to attend to a man who is inebriated, at home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges the letters of SEE MAN TO IT.
explanation.definitionFit: A maisonette is a self-contained flat on two floors, a type of dwelling.

clue.text: Really want to have break such as academics get

parts.note: to long for something is to want it badly
a vacation is a break from work

explanation.surface: Someone yearning for a holiday as long as university staff enjoy.
explanation.walkthrough: The LONG VACATION is the summer break at British universities and law courts; 'break' plays a part in both wordplay and the sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Universities and law courts in Britain have an extended summer recess for staff and students.

clue.text: Sponsor priest to support what he believes in

indicators.note: in a down clue, supporting means the priest's word sits beneath the other

parts.note: a priest believes in God
Father is the title of a Catholic priest

explanation.surface: A backer urging a clergyman to defend his faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to support' sets FATHER under GOD in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A godparent at baptism vouches for the child, standing as a sponsor.

clue.text: Part of hospital has space for officers' mess

parts.note: a ward is a section of a hospital
room means space

explanation.surface: A hospital department with room enough for staff dining.
explanation.definitionFit: On a warship, the commissioned officers eat in this compartment, their mess.

clue.text: Appropriate, your secret

parts.note: to appropriate is to take for oneself, steal
thy is the old form of your

explanation.surface: Take your hidden thing for yourself.
explanation.definitionFit: Stealthy means furtive, done covertly so as not to be noticed.

clue.text: Examination to see if one is fit for work

definitions.text: Examination to see if one is fit for work

parts.words: Examination to see if one is fit for work
parts.note: fit suggests health, but this assessment measures suitability or talent for a job

explanation.surface: A medical check of whether someone is well enough to go back to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fit' suggests a medical; the test is of natural ability, not health.
explanation.definitionFit: A test assessing a candidate's natural talent for a role checks suitability, not health.

clue.text: Graduate takes a season to find rock

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate
to salt food is to season it

explanation.surface: A graduate spends a season looking for stone.
explanation.definitionFit: Basalt is a dark volcanic stone.

clue.text: Maintain one's not to fall behind

definitions.meaning: to sustain or continue something, as in keeping standards high
to stay level with others moving ahead

explanation.surface: An insistence on keeping pace.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrasal verb means both to sustain a level and to stay abreast of rivals.

clue.text: What's passed on is utterly dull

definitions.meaning: passed on is a euphemism for died
a ... sound or colour is flat and lifeless, as in ... boring

explanation.surface: An inheritance that proves thoroughly boring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'passed on' suggests handing down; here it means died.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has passed on has died, and a lifeless, flat thing is also described this way.

clue.text: Saint takes blow, one forcing horse's head down

parts.note: St Martin of Tours is a well-known saint
a gale is a strong blow of wind

explanation.surface: A holy man receives a blow from someone pushing a horse's head down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blow' suggests a punch; it is wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A martingale is a strap of harness that stops a horse raising its head too high.

clue.text: Garden bird, companion for little one

parts.note: the tit is a common garden bird
CH is Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A garden bird keeping a child company.
explanation.walkthrough: CH, Companion of Honour, is a British honour.
explanation.definitionFit: Titch is British slang for a small person, especially a child.

clue.text: Help on a Verdi production

indicators.note: in a down clue, on means the letter A comes after, below, the help word

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: Assistance for staging an opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Aida is an opera by Giuseppe Verdi set in ancient Egypt.

clue.text: Speak up, and cleverly defeat strike

parts.note: to outwit is to beat by cunning
hit means strike

explanation.surface: Urging someone to talk, then outsmart and hit an opponent.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom urges someone to say plainly what they mean.

clue.text: Penny on public transport? Walk

indicators.note: in an across clue, on means the penny goes after the transport word

parts.note: a tram is a form of public transport

explanation.surface: A coin on a bus? Better to go on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily or trek a long way.

clue.text: Spring attractive in upmarket district

parts.note: May is a spring month
fair means attractive

explanation.surface: A good-looking spring season in an expensive area.
explanation.walkthrough: MAYFAIR is a wealthy area of central London.
explanation.definitionFit: Mayfair is an exclusive, expensive area of London's West End.

clue.text: I hear he'll broach last of drink

indicators.note: I hear says the phrase is said aloud

parts.note: he'll is said like heel, and to broach a cask is to tap it

explanation.surface: Someone overhearing that a man will open a cask for the dregs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I hear' signals the sound: 'he'll tap', with broach meaning tap a cask, is said the same as the word for dregs.
explanation.definitionFit: A heeltap is the dregs left at the bottom of a glass.
